# Working with Data in R {#sec-working-with-data}

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: true
# console() renders a code listing plus the console session it produces.
source("_console.R")
suppressMessages({library(dplyr); library(readr); library(tidyr); library(tibble)})
# Examples in this chapter run against this data frame. Students load it
# themselves with read_csv("data/field_yields.csv"); the path differs here
# because the book renders from the project root.
yields <- readr::read_csv("practice/data/field_yields.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

With R installed and the basics in hand, this chapter is about working with real data:
setting up a project folder, installing the tidyverse, reading a CSV file, computing
summary statistics, and getting a dataset into a shape you can analyze.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Set up a self-contained project folder that someone else can open and run.
2. Install and load packages, and explain the difference between the two.
3. Read a CSV file into R as a data frame, and diagnose file-not-found errors.
4. Explore a dataset in Positron's Data Explorer.
5. Compute summary statistics in R, handling missing values correctly.
6. Explain what "tidy data" means, and reshape a dataset with `pivot_longer` and `pivot_wider`.
7. Clean up awkward column names.
:::

## One Folder Per Project {#sec-project-folder}

Before reading any data into R, set up a folder to work in. R always has a **working
directory** -- the folder it treats as "here" -- and most file problems come from R looking
in a different place than you expect. The fix is a habit: keep each analysis in its own
folder, and open that folder in Positron.

A layout that works for almost everything:

```
canola-trial/
  data/
    canola_trial.csv          <- exactly as it arrived
  R/
    01_clean.R
    02_analysis.R
  output/
    yield_by_variety.png
    summary_table.csv
  README.md
```

**The project is self-contained.**  Everything the analysis needs is inside `canola-trial/`.
You can zip the folder, send it to somebody, and it will run on their machine.  A script that
reaches out to a file elsewhere on your hard drive will not.

**Raw data is never edited.**  `data/` holds the file as it arrived.  If you open the CSV in
Excel, fix three cells and save, you have written over the only copy of what you were given,
and there is no record of what you changed.  Do the fixing in the script, where it leaves a
trail.

**Outputs are disposable.**  Anything in `output/` can be deleted and regenerated by re-running
the scripts.  That is a useful test: delete `output/`, run the scripts, and see whether
everything comes back.

**Scripts are numbered in the order they run.**  `01_clean.R` then `02_analysis.R`.  Six months
later this tells you where to start.

To make the working directory be your project folder, open the folder in Positron with
**File → Open Folder…**.  Do this at the start of every session.

One more reason for the habit: AI coding assistants read the files in your project folder to
understand your data and scripts. We return to this in Module 5.

## Paths, and Why `setwd()` Is a Trap {#sec-paths}

A path tells R where a file is.  There are two kinds.

An **absolute path** starts at the root of your hard drive:

```r
read_csv("/Users/peter/Documents/canola-trial/data/canola_trial.csv")
```

A **relative path** starts wherever R currently is:

```r
read_csv("data/canola_trial.csv")
```

The relative version works on any machine where the project folder is open.  The absolute one
works only on mine, because it names a user, a folder layout and an operating system that your
classmate does not share.

R does have a function, `setwd()`, that changes the working directory from inside a script:

```r
setwd("/Users/peter/Documents/canola-trial")     # do not do this
```

This is the most common reason a script that works fine for its author fails
for everyone else.  It writes one machine into a file you are going to share.  Open the project
folder instead, and plain relative paths work.

One wrinkle.  Windows paths use backslashes, as in `C:\Users\...`, but a backslash means
something special inside an R string.  Write forward slashes even on Windows: `"C:/Users/..."`.
R handles the translation.

## File Names {#sec-file-names}

Two rules save a lot of trouble.

Avoid spaces and punctuation.  `yield data (final).csv` will work until the day it does not.
`yield_data_final.csv` is safer.

Write dates as YYYY-MM-DD.  `2025-09-15_deliveries.csv` sorts chronologically on its own, and
`Sept15.csv` does not.

If you find yourself writing `final`, `final_v2`, `final_REAL` in file names, the project needs
a way of tracking versions rather than a longer file name.  Version control systems do this,
and Git is the common one.  It is worth learning if you carry on with this kind of work,
though we will not cover it here.

## Packages {#sec-packages}

A **package** is a bundle of extra functions someone has written that do not come with R
itself. The one we will use most is the **tidyverse**, described in the next section.
Using a package is a two-step process:

1. **Install it -- once per computer.** This downloads the package from the internet and saves it on your machine. You only ever do this once (per computer):

    ```r
    install.packages("tidyverse")
    ```

    This prints a *lot* of text -- progress bars and messages, sometimes in red. That red text is normal; it is not an error. Just wait for it to finish (it can take a few minutes the first time).

2. **Load it -- once per script.** Installing puts the package on your computer, but it is not switched on until you *load* it. Put this at the top of every script that uses the tidyverse:

    ```r
    library(tidyverse)
    ```

If you skip the `library()` step and try to use a tidyverse function, R will stop with an error like:

```
Error in read_csv(...) : could not find function "read_csv"
```

That "could not find function" message almost always means you forgot to load the package (or you have not installed it yet). The fix is to run `library(tidyverse)` first. Note the quirk: you put quotes around the name when you *install* (`install.packages("tidyverse")`) but not when you *load* (`library(tidyverse)`).

## The Tidyverse {#sec-tidyverse}

The **tidyverse** is a collection of packages that share a common design: `readr` reads data,
`dplyr` manipulates it, `tidyr` reshapes it, and `ggplot2` graphs it, among others.
Installing the tidyverse installs the whole collection, and `library(tidyverse)` loads the
core packages at once. It has become the standard way of working with tabular data in R, and
it is what this book uses.

Base R can do most of the same things, and you will sometimes see base functions in other
people's code or in AI-generated code. The two styles mix fine; we simply teach the tidyverse
versions.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Other resources — packages and the tidyverse

- **R for Data Science (2nd ed.)** -- the [Introduction](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/intro.html) describes the tidyverse workflow (import → tidy → transform → visualize → model → communicate) this course follows.
- **tidyverse.org** -- [the package index](https://www.tidyverse.org/packages/) lists the core packages and what each does.
:::

## Reading Data from CSV {#sec-reading-data}

The dataset for this chapter and the next is
[`field_yields.csv`](practice/data/field_yields.csv) -- 60 canola fields with columns
`field_id`, `region`, `variety`, `acres`, `yield_bu_acre`, `year`, `seeding_date`, and
`units`. Download it and put it in your project's `data/` folder.

Once the tidyverse is loaded, you can read it:

```r
yields <- read_csv("data/field_yields.csv")
```

`read_csv` reads the file into a data frame and saves it in the object `yields`. It also
prints a short note about what column types it guessed -- check them, because R guesses well
but not perfectly.

The path `"data/field_yields.csv"` is relative: R starts from the working directory and
looks for a `data/` folder inside it. If you opened your project folder
(@sec-project-folder), that is exactly where the file is, and this just works. If R cannot
find the file, you get:

```
Error: 'data/field_yields.csv' does not exist in current working directory (...)
```

Two things to check, in order:

- **Did you open the project folder?** **File → Open Folder…** in Positron, then pick the
  folder that contains `data/`.
- **Where does R think it is?** Run `getwd()` ("get working directory"). It prints the folder
  R is currently using; the error message shows it too.

A couple more notes:

- If your file uses semicolons or tabs instead of commas, use `read_csv2` or `read_tsv`.
- To save a data frame back out, `write_csv(yields, "output/yields_clean.csv")` is the
  mirror image of `read_csv`.

Once you have the data in, you can explore it:

```r
yields              # prints the data frame (first 10 rows)
head(yields)        # first 6 rows
tail(yields)        # last 6 rows
nrow(yields)        # number of rows
ncol(yields)        # number of columns
names(yields)       # column names
glimpse(yields)     # compact column-by-column view, with types
summary(yields)     # quick summary of every column
```

`summary()` is especially useful as a first look at a new dataset. For every numeric column it reports the min, max, mean, median, and quartiles; for text columns it simply notes how many values there are. Always run it when you open a new dataset.

### Viewing Data in Positron {#sec-data-explorer .unnumbered}

Positron also lets you *look* at a data frame the way you would in Excel. After you run the
`read_csv` line, `yields` appears in the **Variables** pane. Click it and Positron opens the
**Data Explorer**: a spreadsheet-style view of the data.

<!-- TODO(Peter): screenshot of the Variables pane with `yields` listed after read_csv.
![After reading the file, `yields` appears in the Variables pane. Clicking it opens the Data Explorer.](images/positron_variables_yields.png){#fig-variables-yields}
-->

<!-- TODO(Peter): screenshot of the Data Explorer open on field_yields.
![The Data Explorer: the data in a spreadsheet-style grid, with a summary column profile down the left.](images/positron_data_explorer.png){#fig-data-explorer}
-->

The Data Explorer has two parts. The grid shows the rows and columns, and you can sort and
filter them by clicking the column headers. The summary panel shows, for each column, its
type, the percentage of missing values, and a small sketch of its distribution.

The Data Explorer is for looking, not editing. You cannot change a cell: the file in `data/`
stays as it arrived, and any fixing happens in the script. When you want the same answers in
code, use `summary()` and `glimpse()`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Summary Statistics in R {#sec-r-summary-stats}

All the summary statistics from Module 1 exist in R too. With the `yields` data frame from
@sec-reading-data loaded:

```r
mean(yields$yield_bu_acre)
median(yields$yield_bu_acre)
sd(yields$yield_bu_acre)
var(yields$yield_bu_acre)
min(yields$yield_bu_acre)
max(yields$yield_bu_acre)
range(yields$yield_bu_acre)              # returns c(min, max)
quantile(yields$yield_bu_acre, 0.25)
quantile(yields$yield_bu_acre, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))  # multiple at once
IQR(yields$yield_bu_acre)
```

One thing to watch for: if your data has **missing values** (coded as `NA` in R), these functions will return `NA` by default. To compute the statistic ignoring the missing values, pass `na.rm = TRUE`:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
console('
mean(yields$yield_bu_acre)

mean(yields$yield_bu_acre, na.rm = TRUE)
')
```

If `mean()` returns `NA` unexpectedly, the first thing to check is whether your data has
missing values. This default is deliberate -- silently ignoring missing values (as Excel
often does) hides a problem you should know about. We return to missing values properly when
we clean data in Module 3.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Tidy Data {#sec-tidy-data}

Hadley Wickham (one of the creators of the tidyverse) has written extensively about what he calls **tidy data** [@r4ds]. A dataset is tidy if:

1. Every variable has its own **column**.
2. Every observation has its own **row**.
3. Every value has its own **cell**.

That sounds obvious, but a huge fraction of real datasets violate it. Common problems:

- **Column headers are values, not variable names.** For example, a table with columns `2020`, `2021`, `2022`, `2023` where each column contains yields. The column header should be a variable called `year`; the values should be in a single `yield` column.
- **Multiple variables in one column.** For example, a `region_variety` column that contains `"South_InVigor"`. These should be two separate columns.
- **Observations split across rows.** For example, one row for price and another for quantity of the same product. These should be columns.

You can do analysis on untidy data, but it is much harder. Almost every tool in the tidyverse assumes tidy input. If your data is not tidy, your first step should usually be to *make* it tidy.

### Reshaping with `pivot_longer` and `pivot_wider` {.unnumbered}

This is the wide-versus-long distinction from @sec-wide-long, where a PivotTable needed the
long form. The same data can be stored wide -- one column per crop -- or long, with the crop
as a variable:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
console('
yields_wide <- tibble(
  region = c("South", "Central", "North"),
  Canola = c(41, 44, 38),
  Wheat  = c(52, 55, 49),
  Barley = c(64, 68, 60)
)
yields_wide
')
```

The wide table is untidy in the first way listed above: the column headers `Canola`, `Wheat`,
`Barley` are values of a variable (crop), not variables themselves. `pivot_longer` fixes it.
You tell it which columns to gather, what to call the column that will hold their *names*, and
what to call the column that will hold their *values*:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
console('
yields_long <- pivot_longer(yields_wide,
                            cols = c(Canola, Wheat, Barley),
                            names_to = "crop",
                            values_to = "yield")
yields_long
')
```

Nine rows now: one per region-crop combination, with `crop` and `yield` as ordinary columns
that R can group and filter on.

`pivot_wider` goes the other way. Tell it which column holds the names and which holds the
values:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
console('
pivot_wider(yields_long, names_from = crop, values_from = yield)
')
```

Long is usually what analysis wants; wide is often what people want to read. Expect to pivot
in both directions -- data from Statistics Canada, for example, typically arrives long and
needs widening for a report table.

When you read in a dataset, look at the shape. Is each row an observation? Is each column a variable? If not, fixing that is the first step.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Renaming and Cleaning Column Names {#sec-renaming}

Real-world datasets often have terrible column names: `Yield (bu/ac)`, `REGION_NAME`, `X1`. These will work in R but are annoying to type and easy to mistype. Clean them up early:

```r
yields <- rename(yields,
                 yield_bu_ac = "Yield (bu/ac)",
                 region = REGION_NAME)
```

For wholesale renaming, use `janitor::clean_names()`. (This is from the `janitor` package, not the tidyverse. Install it once with `install.packages("janitor")`.)

```r
library(janitor)
yields <- clean_names(read_csv("data/messy_data.csv"))
```

`clean_names` converts everything to lowercase with underscores and strips special characters. Run it on almost anything you read in.
